claim: Many proteins undergo a process of phase separation that leads to the formation of biomolecular condensates.
source: Many proteins have been recently shown to undergo a process of phase separation that leads to the formation of biomolecular condensates.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this phenomenon.

claim: Some proteins form dense droplets of sizeable dimensions below the critical concentration for phase separation.
source: Intriguingly, it has been observed that some of these proteins form dense droplets of sizeable dimensions already below the critical concentration, which is the concentration at which phase separation occurs.
evidence: This observation is stated as empirical evidence from prior studies.

claim: The formation of sizeable droplets below the critical concentration is not readily compatible with classical nucleation theory.
source: To understand this phenomenon, which is not readily compatible with classical nucleation theory, we investigated the properties of the droplet size distributions as a function of protein concentration.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with established nucleation theory.

claim: Droplet size distributions can be described by a scale-invariant log-normal function with an average that increases progressively as the concentration approaches the critical concentration from below.
source: We found that these distributions can be described by a scale-invariant log-normal function with an average that increases progressively as the concentration approaches the critical concentration from below.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on analysis of experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The scaling analysis suggests the existence of a universal behaviour independent of the sequences and structures of the proteins undergoing phase separation.
source: The results of this scaling analysis suggest the existence of a universal behaviour independent of the sequences and structures of the proteins undergoing phase separation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the scaling analysis results.

claim: Scale invariance can be used to estimate the critical concentration for protein phase separation.
source: Furthermore, based on these observations, we show that it is possible to use the scale invariance to estimate the critical concentration for protein phase separation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Protein phase separation may lead to the formation of biomolecular condensates of physiological significance.
source: This process appears to be of physiological significance since it may lead to the formation of biomolecular condensates (Brangwynne et al., 2009; Hyman et al., 2014; Banani et al., 2017; Alberti and Hyman, 2021; Lyon et al., 2021; Buchan and Parker, 2009; Andersen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Protein phase separation is closely controlled by the protein homeostasis system.
source: As a consequence, it is closely controlled by the protein homeostasis system (Mateju et al., 2017; Qamar et al., 2018), and its dysregulation has been associated with a broad range of human diseases (Mitrea et al., 2022; Vendruscolo and Fuxreiter, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dysregulation of protein phase separation has been associated with a broad range of human diseases.
source: As a consequence, it is closely controlled by the protein homeostasis system (Mateju et al., 2017; Qamar et al., 2018), and its dysregulation has been associated with a broad range of human diseases (Mitrea et al., 2022; Vendruscolo and Fuxreiter, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Proteins can form droplets of sizeable dimensions well below the concentration at which phase separation occurs.
source: This question appears as a promising starting point to develop new insights since it has been reported that proteins can form droplets of sizeable dimensions already well below the concentration at which phase separation occurs (Stender et al., 2021; Kar et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific experimental studies.

claim: The behaviour of forming sizeable droplets below the critical concentration is not predicted by classical nucleation theory.
source: This behaviour is not predicted by classical nucleation theory (Li et al., 2012), and not readily consistent with the idea that the protein phase separation process can be described as a first-order phase transition.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with established theory and citation.

claim: In a first-order phase transition, nucleation takes place in a supersaturated system.
source: This is because, in a first-order phase transition, nucleation takes place in a supersaturated system (Shimobayashi et al., 2021), while in a subsaturated system particles can still self-assemble, but with a probability that decreases exponentially with the size of the assemblies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about phase transitions, supported by citation.

claim: In a subsaturated system, particles can still self-assemble, but with a probability that decreases exponentially with the size of the assemblies.
source: This is because, in a first-order phase transition, nucleation takes place in a supersaturated system (Shimobayashi et al., 2021), while in a subsaturated system particles can still self-assemble, but with a probability that decreases exponentially with the size of the assemblies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about phase transitions, supported by citation.

claim: The droplet size distributions of FUS and α-synuclein follow a scale-invariant log-normal behaviour.
source: We report the observation that the droplet size distributions of the proteins FUS and α-synuclein follow a scale-invariant log-normal behaviour.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data analysis.

claim: The findings are consistent with a universal behaviour resulting from the presence of an increasingly large correlation length as the concentration approaches the critical concentration from below.
source: These findings are consistent with a universal behaviour resulting from the presence of an increasingly large correlation length, ξ, as the concentration approaches the critical concentration from below.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The correlation length is related to the typical spatial range over which density fluctuations are correlated.
source: The correlation length is an emergent characteristic, and it is related to the typical spatial range over which density fluctuations are correlated.
evidence: This is established knowledge about correlation length in statistical physics.

claim: When the correlation length is sufficiently large, scale invariance and finite-size scaling can occur within a range of lengths spanning from the molecular size to the correlation length.
source: When ξ is sufficiently large, one can expect scale invariance and finite-size scaling (Brankov et al., 2000) to occur within a range of lengths spanning from the molecular size to ξ.
evidence: This is established knowledge about scaling phenomena, supported by citation.

claim: Physical observables cease to depend explicitly on numerous microscopic details when the correlation length is large, leading to universal behaviour.
source: This means that physical observables cease to depend explicitly on numerous microscopic details that are peculiar to spatial scales smaller than ξ, thus leading to a universal behaviour characterized by quantities obtained by coarse graining over scales smaller than ξ.
evidence: This is established knowledge about universality in statistical physics.

claim: At a first-order phase transition, the correlation length is finite.
source: At a first-order phase transition, ξ is finite, and if it is not large enough, the length range discussed above remains too short to observe scale invariance.
evidence: This is established knowledge about first-order phase transitions.

claim: The vicinity of the spinodal line to the coexistence curve might cause a large increase of the correlation length as the first-order phase transition is approached by increasing the concentration.
source: However, the vicinity of the spinodal line, where nucleation disappears as the dilute phase becomes unstable, to the coexistence curve, where nucleation appears as the dilute phase becomes metastable, might cause a large increase of ξ as the first-order phase transition is approached by increasing the concentration.
evidence: This is a theoretical speculation based on phase transition theory.

claim: If not preceded by a first-order phase transition, the spinodal line would correspond to a second-order phase transition, resulting in infinite correlation length.
source: If it is not preceded by a first-order phase transition, the spinodal line would correspond to a second-order phase transition, resulting in infinite ξ, with scale invariance holding on all length scales larger than the molecular scale.
evidence: This is established knowledge about second-order phase transitions.

claim: The scaling analysis exhibits a high degree of generality, devoid of reliance on specific underlying models.
source: Nevertheless, our scaling analysis exhibits a high degree of generality, devoid of reliance on specific underlying models.
evidence: This is a characterization of the analysis approach used in the study.

claim: Close to the critical concentration, the timescale required for the equilibration of a system grows together with the correlation length, exceeding the timescale amenable to experimental observation.
source: Such challenge arises from the fact that close to the critical concentration, the timescale required for the equilibration of a system grows together with ξ, thus exceeding the timescale amenable to experimental observation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about critical phenomena.

claim: Scale invariance holds near the coexistence curve for the droplet size distributions.
source: Our analysis of experimental data indicates that: (i) scale invariance does indeed hold near the coexistence curve and (ii) the droplet size distribution is log-normal.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data analysis.

claim: The droplet size distribution is log-normal.
source: Our analysis of experimental data indicates that: (i) scale invariance does indeed hold near the coexistence curve and (ii) the droplet size distribution is log-normal.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data analysis.

claim: Methods to assess the critical concentration are crucial for understanding the location of proteins in their phase diagram.
source: Finally, we note that methods to assess the critical concentration are crucial for understanding the location of proteins in their phase diagram, their proximity to the phase boundary between the native and droplet states, and how pharmacological interventions can modify their phase behaviour.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of the methodology.

claim: An accurate estimate of the critical concentration is possible based on measurements carried out away from the critical point, where experimental errors are smaller.
source: In this way, an accurate estimate of the critical concentration is possible because it is based on measurements carried out away from the critical point, under conditions such that fluctuations are small, and hence experimental errors are smaller than in the proximity of the transition.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the proposed method.

claim: Protein self-assembly into liquid-like condensates is characterized by a phase separation transition at a concentration ρc.
source: Empirical evidence indicates that protein self-assembly into liquid-like condensates is characterized by: (i) a phase separation transition at a concentration ρc , (ii) a formation of droplets of sizeable dimensions already below ρc , and (iii) a droplet size distribution that, after an initial transient, does not change with the experimental observation time, although individual droplets can form, grow, shrink, and dissolve.
evidence: This is stated as empirical evidence from observations.

claim: Protein self-assembly into liquid-like condensates is characterized by formation of droplets of sizeable dimensions already below ρc.
source: Empirical evidence indicates that protein self-assembly into liquid-like condensates is characterized by: (i) a phase separation transition at a concentration ρc , (ii) a formation of droplets of sizeable dimensions already below ρc , and (iii) a droplet size distribution that, after an initial transient, does not change with the experimental observation time, although individual droplets can form, grow, shrink, and dissolve.
evidence: This is stated as empirical evidence from observations.

claim: After an initial transient, the droplet size distribution does not change with the experimental observation time, although individual droplets can form, grow, shrink, and dissolve.
source: Empirical evidence indicates that protein self-assembly into liquid-like condensates is characterized by: (i) a phase separation transition at a concentration ρc , (ii) a formation of droplets of sizeable dimensions already below ρc , and (iii) a droplet size distribution that, after an initial transient, does not change with the experimental observation time, although individual droplets can form, grow, shrink, and dissolve.
evidence: This is stated as empirical evidence from observations.

claim: The scaling approach is analogous to analysing the cluster size distribution in a percolation problem.
source: We also note that this approach is analogous to analysing the cluster size distribution in a percolation problem (Stauffer and Aharony, 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to established methods, supported by citation.

claim: The characteristic size sc is defined as the ratio of the second to the first moment of the droplet size distribution.
source: The characteristic size sc is defined, apart from a proportionality constant (see below), as the ratio of the second to the first moment of the droplet size distribution.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the manuscript.

claim: Critical exponents are expected to be universal, independent of specific details of the system.
source: A consequence of scaling and singular behaviour described by Equation 2, that is the divergence of the characteristic size of the droplets, is that details of any specific system may not affect the value of the critical exponents, which are therefore expected to be universal, that is independent of specific details of the system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about universality in critical phenomena.

claim: The critical concentration ρc for untagged FUS is 5.0 μM.
source: We used the estimates of the critical concentrations, ρc = 5.0 μM for FUS and ρc = 5.4 μM for SNAP-tagged FUS, obtained below, in a self-consistency check of the validity of the scaling ansatz.
evidence: This is a value determined from the analysis in the manuscript.

claim: The critical concentration ρc for SNAP-tagged FUS is 5.4 μM.
source: We used the estimates of the critical concentrations, ρc = 5.0 μM for FUS and ρc = 5.4 μM for SNAP-tagged FUS, obtained below, in a self-consistency check of the validity of the scaling ansatz.
evidence: This is a value determined from the analysis in the manuscript.

claim: The moment ratios at different distances from the critical concentration fall onto straight lines for FUS.
source: We observed that the moment ratios at different distances from the critical concentration fall onto straight lines, as predicted by the scaling ansatz.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis, shown in Figure 1.

claim: The weighted average slope of the lines for different moment ratios is 0.95 ± 0.05 for untagged FUS.
source: In addition, the weighted average slope (see Equations 15 and 16 below) of the lines for different moment ratios is 0.95 ± 0.05 for untagged FUS, and 0.95 ± 0.05 for SNAP-tagged FUS, which is in good agreement with φ = 1 for the exponent in the scaling ansatz in Equation 1 (Figure 1A, C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from data analysis, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The weighted average slope of the lines for different moment ratios is 0.95 ± 0.05 for SNAP-tagged FUS.
source: In addition, the weighted average slope (see Equations 15 and 16 below) of the lines for different moment ratios is 0.95 ± 0.05 for untagged FUS, and 0.95 ± 0.05 for SNAP-tagged FUS, which is in good agreement with φ = 1 for the exponent in the scaling ansatz in Equation 1 (Figure 1A, C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from data analysis, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The exponent φ is approximately 1 for FUS.
source: In addition, the weighted average slope (see Equations 15 and 16 below) of the lines for different moment ratios is 0.95 ± 0.05 for untagged FUS, and 0.95 ± 0.05 for SNAP-tagged FUS, which is in good agreement with φ = 1 for the exponent in the scaling ansatz in Equation 1 (Figure 1A, C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: Using the value of φ = 1, the exponent α = 0 for FUS.
source: Using the value of φ = 1, determined based on Equation 4, we obtain α = 0.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the determined value of φ and the slope m.

claim: The data support the validity of the scaling ansatz of Equation 1 for FUS.
source: Taken together, these data support the validity of the scaling ansatz of Equation 1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results.

claim: The droplet size distribution of FUS may follow a log-normal distribution.
source: The above analysis suggests that the droplet size distribution may follow a log-normal distribution.
evidence: This is an inference from the scaling analysis.

claim: The size distribution functions for both untagged FUS and SNAP-tagged FUS collapse when rescaled, consistent with log-normal behaviour.
source: We observed that the size distribution functions collapsed for both FUS and SNAP-tagged FUS (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The collapsed curve overlaps with the analytic log-normal distribution computed with s0 = 1, σ = 1.
source: Furthermore, the collapsed curve overlapped with the analytic log-normal distribution we computed with s0 = 1, σ = 1, the normal distribution in the rescaled variables.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The observed collapse supports that droplet size distributions from different experiments follow a log-normal behaviour.
source: The observed collapse supports the observation that droplet size distributions from different experiments follows a log-normal behaviour.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collapse analysis.

claim: The σ values are nearly uniform at different concentrations for FUS, with the exception of data at the lowest concentration values.
source: This prediction is verified in Figure 2B, where the σ (Hyman et al., 2014) values are shown to be nearly uniform at different concentrations, with the exception of the data at the lowest concentration values, that is those furthest away from the critical concentration.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The line should intersect the ρ-axis at the critical concentration, providing an estimate of ρc.
source: It is important to note that this is the consequence only of the scaling ansatz and not of the log-normal distribution. The line should intersect the ρ-axis at the critical concentration providing an estimate of ρc.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction that can be used to estimate ρc.

claim: The average of the estimated ρc values is 5.0 ± 0.2 μM for FUS.
source: The average of the estimated ρc values is 5.0 ± 0.2 μM for FUS and 5.4 ± 0.4 μM for SNAP-tagged FUS (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis, shown in Figure 3.

claim: The average of the estimated ρc values is 5.4 ± 0.4 μM for SNAP-tagged FUS.
source: The average of the estimated ρc values is 5.0 ± 0.2 μM for FUS and 5.4 ± 0.4 μM for SNAP-tagged FUS (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis, shown in Figure 3.

claim: Both estimates of ρc are higher than the values originally reported (ρc = 2 μM of untagged and ρc = 3 μM of tagged FUS).
source: Both estimates are higher than the values of ρc originally reported (ρc = 2 μM of untagged and ρc = 3 μM of tagged FUS; Kar et al., 2022) but consistent with them once taken into account the behaviour of the plateau of the absorbance of a spin-down assay used in that work.
evidence: This is a comparison with previously reported values, with citation.

claim: The estimates of ρc are compatible with other ones recently reported.
source: We also note that our estimates are compatible with other ones recently reported (Patel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with other reported values, with citation.

claim: The SDFs collapsed with the estimated value of ρc for both untagged and tagged FUS.
source: We observed that both in cases of untagged and tagged FUS, the SDFs collapsed with our estimated value of ρc (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis, shown in Figure 4.

claim: The scaling model can be used to estimate the critical concentration based on the distribution of droplet sizes.
source: These results indicate that the scaling model can be used to estimate the critical concentration based on the distribution of droplet sizes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results.

claim: α-synuclein forms droplets (called clusters) below the critical concentration.
source: As α-synuclein droplets (called clusters) were recently reported below the critical concentration (Ray et al., 2023), we aimed at characterizing whether such droplets also follow scale-invariant size distribution.
evidence: This is stated as a recent observation from cited literature.

claim: Droplet sizes of α-synuclein were measured at 5% PEG concentration 10 min after detection of liquid-like condensates using increasing concentrations of α-synuclein (20, 40, 50, 60, 75, 80, and 100 μM).
source: We measured droplet sizes at 5% PEG concentration 10 min after detection of liquid-like condensates using increasing concentrations of α-synuclein (20, 40, 50, 60, 75, 80, and 100 μM) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used.

claim: For α-synuclein, the critical exponent φ = 1.3 ± 0.2.
source: Using k values of 0.25, 0.75, 1.25, 1.75, the critical exponents in the scaling ansatz (Equations 4 and 6), obtaining φ = 1.3 ± 0.2 (Figure 5A) and m = 1 − α = 0.9 ± 0.2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: For α-synuclein, m = 1 − α = 0.9 ± 0.2.
source: Using k values of 0.25, 0.75, 1.25, 1.75, the critical exponents in the scaling ansatz (Equations 4 and 6), obtaining φ = 1.3 ± 0.2 (Figure 5A) and m = 1 − α = 0.9 ± 0.2 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: As control, the critical exponents for α-synuclein were determined using Equation 19, obtaining φ = 1.1 ± 0.2 and m = 1 − α = 0.8 ± 0.2.
source: As control, we also determined the critical exponents using the scaling ansatz in a different way, using Equation 19, obtaining φ = 1.1 ± 0.2 and m = 1 − α = 0.8 ± 0.2, corroborating the validity of the scale-invariant model.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from an alternative analysis method.

claim: The critical concentration for α-synuclein is ρc = 137 ± 10 μM using Equation 18.
source: We then estimated the critical concentration using the two methods obtaining ρc = 137 ± 10 μM, using Equation 18 (Figure 5C) and ρc = 125 ± 7 μM, using Equation 19 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The critical concentration for α-synuclein is ρc = 125 ± 7 μM using Equation 19.
source: We then estimated the critical concentration using the two methods obtaining ρc = 137 ± 10 μM, using Equation 18 (Figure 5C) and ρc = 125 ± 7 μM, using Equation 19 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis, shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The droplet size distributions of α-synuclein are stationary below the critical concentration.
source: The droplet size distributions are stationary below the critical concentration, as expected (Figure 6B, C; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the data, shown in Figure 6B, C.

claim: It is unclear whether the droplets observed below the saturation concentration and those detected above result from the same process.
source: For example, it is unclear whether the droplets observed below the saturation concentration and those detected above result from the same process.
evidence: This is a statement about current uncertainty in the field.

claim: Scale invariance means that the description of the behaviour of a system remains the same regardless of the scale of observation.
source: Scale invariance means that the description of the behaviour of a system remains the same regardless of the scale of observation.
evidence: This is a definition of scale invariance.

claim: Scale invariance has been seen in self-similar systems like fractals, which repeat patterns at different length scales.
source: It has been seen for example in self-similar systems like fractals, which repeat patterns at different length scales (Song et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an example of scale invariance, supported by citation.

claim: Scale invariance is commonly observed in physics, biology, and economics.
source: Scale invariance is commonly observed in physics, biology, and economics, where it helps understand complex systems by identifying consistent patterns and fundamental properties (Stanley, 1999).
evidence: This is a general statement about scale invariance, supported by citation.

claim: The critical exponents of the scaling model are the same for different systems.
source: The critical exponents of the scaling model are the same for different systems.
evidence: This is a statement about universality observed in the analysis.

claim: The log-normal model is general for nucleation and grain size growth ranging from crystal seeding to the mass size distributions in organism growth of various sea organisms.
source: We also note the generality of the log-normal model for nucleation and grain size growth ranging from crystal seeding (Binder and Virnau, 2016; Bergmann and Bill, 2008) to the mass size distributions in organism growth of various sea organisms (Giometto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the generality of log-normal distributions, supported by citations.

claim: The Flory–Huggins theory describes a first-order phase separation in a system of homopolymers.
source: In its simplest form, this theory describes a first-order phase separation in a system of homopolymers, which can also be adapted to polyampholites (Overbeek and Voorn, 1957).
evidence: This is a description of the Flory-Huggins theory, supported by citation.

claim: The Flory–Huggins theory has been extended to associative polymers by Flory and Stockmayer, who described the phase separation in terms of a third-order gelation process.
source: The Flory–Huggins theory has been extended to associative polymers, with the aim of modelling the sequence composition of proteins, by Flory and Stockmayer, who described the phase separation in terms of a third-order gelation process (Flory, 1941; Stockmayer, 1943).
evidence: This is a description of an extension of the theory, supported by citations.

claim: Semenov and Rubinstein reported that the gelation process is not a real phase transition, as all the derivatives of the free energy are analytical at the gelation point.
source: Semenov and Rubinstein modified the Flory–Stockmayer theory, reporting that the gelation process is not a real phase transition, as all the derivatives of the free energy are analytical at the gelation point (Semenov and Rubinstein, 1998).
evidence: This is a description of a modification to the theory, supported by citation.

claim: γ-crystallin was reported to undergo a second-order phase separation process.
source: In an older study, γ-crystallin was reported to undergo a second-order phase separation process (Thomson et al., 1987), consistently with observations in lysozyme solutions (Ishimoto and Tanaka, 1977).
evidence: This is a description of a prior observation, supported by citations.

claim: It has been suggested that the protein phase separation process is coupled with percolation.
source: More recently, it has been suggested that the protein phase separation process is coupled with percolation (Mittag and Pappu, 2022).
evidence: This is a description of a recent suggestion, supported by citation.

claim: Percolation models exhibit a continuous transition marked by a diverging correlation length and a scale-invariant droplet size distribution.
source: It is notable that percolation models exhibit a continuous transition marked by a diverging correlation length and a scale-invariant droplet size distribution (Stauffer and Aharony, 2018), resembling the general form as presented in Equations 1 and 2.
evidence: This is a description of percolation models, supported by citation.

claim: The critical exponents for 3D percolation at the critical threshold are α = 1.19 and φ = 2.21.
source: However, the critical exponents for 3D percolation at the critical threshold are α = 1.19 and φ = 2.21, and in mean-field (d > 6) scenarios, they are α = 1.5 and φ = 2, as per existing literature (Stauffer and Aharony, 2018).
evidence: This is a statement of known values from percolation theory, supported by citation.

claim: In mean-field (d > 6) percolation scenarios, the critical exponents are α = 1.5 and φ = 2.
source: However, the critical exponents for 3D percolation at the critical threshold are α = 1.19 and φ = 2.21, and in mean-field (d > 6) scenarios, they are α = 1.5 and φ = 2, as per existing literature (Stauffer and Aharony, 2018).
evidence: This is a statement of known values from percolation theory, supported by citation.

claim: The scaling analysis is consistent with α = 0 and φ = 1, which differs from standard percolation exponents.
source: In contrast, our scaling analysis is consistent with α = 0 and φ = 1.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis, contrasting with percolation theory.

claim: A phase separation coupled with percolation model could be consistent with the scaling behaviour if this coupling would induce a shift in the universality class from that of standard percolation.
source: Therefore, a phase separation coupled with percolation model (Mittag and Pappu, 2022) could be consistent with the scaling behaviour reported here if this coupling would induce a shift in the universality class from that of standard percolation (Stauffer and Aharony, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation about how percolation models might be reconciled with the findings.

claim: When the correlation length exceeds the cellular dimensions, the remnants of what should have been a first-order phase transition in an infinite system may effectively exhibit indistinguishable characteristics from a second-order phase transition.
source: In such cases, however, when the correlation length exceeds the cellular dimensions, the remnants of what should have been a first-order phase transition in an infinite system may effectively exhibit indistinguishable characteristics from a second-order phase transition.
evidence: This is a theoretical speculation about finite-size effects.

claim: A power law distribution has recently been reported for nucleoli above the transition temperature.
source: We also note that a power law distribution, but above the transition temperature, has recently been reported for nucleoli (Lee et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a reference to a recent observation, supported by citation.

claim: The existence of scale invariance for the droplet size distribution imposes stringent constraints on theoretical models that aim to elucidate protein phase separation.
source: Quite generally, the existence of scale invariance for the droplet size distribution, at least under the conditions investigated, imposes stringent constraints on theoretical models that aim to elucidate protein phase separation.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the findings.

claim: The importance of a scaling analysis lies in its ability to uncover the fundamental aspects of universal phenomena, transcending models confined solely to specific systems.
source: The importance of a scaling analysis lies in its ability to uncover the fundamental aspects of universal phenomena, transcending models confined solely to specific systems for which they were originally designed.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of the scaling approach.

claim: The moments of the droplet size distribution can be used to obtain an estimate of the critical concentration for phase separation.
source: As a practical consequence of the scaling model, the moments of the droplet size distribution can be used to obtain an estimate of the critical concentration for phase separation.
evidence: This is a practical application of the findings.

claim: It has been challenging to determine critical concentrations in the study of protein phase separation, particularly in cell systems.
source: It has been challenging to determine critical concentrations in the study of protein phase separation, particularly in cell systems.
evidence: This is a statement about a challenge in the field.

claim: It remains unclear when observed protein droplets are formed at subsaturation concentrations versus supersaturation concentrations.
source: As a consequence, it remains still largely unclear when the observed protein droplets are formed at subsaturation concentrations, and when they represent phase-separated condensates at supersaturation concentrations.
evidence: This is a statement about current uncertainty in the field.

claim: The scale-invariant log-normal behaviour offers a tool to determine the critical concentration.
source: The scale-invariant log-normal behaviour that we have reported offers a tool to determine the critical concentration.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the findings.

claim: This approach should enable the positioning of a system with respect to the phase boundary when experimental data could be obtained about the length (1D), area (2D), or volume (3D) of the condensates.
source: This approach should enable the positioning of a system with respect to the phase boundary when experimental data could be obtained about the length (1D), area (2D), or volume (3D) of the condensates.
evidence: This is a prediction about the applicability of the method.

claim: This method will find applications in the study of protein condensates in the cell.
source: We anticipate that this method will find applications in the study of protein condensates in the cell.
evidence: This is a prediction about future applications.

claim: The scale invariance of the droplet size distribution is characteristic of critical phenomena, which tend to be highly sensitive to environmental conditions.
source: We also note that the scale invariance of the droplet size distribution that we have reported is characteristic of critical phenomena, which tend to be highly sensitive to environmental conditions.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of critical phenomena.

claim: The formation and dimensions of protein droplets could be rather tunable.
source: The formation and dimensions of protein droplets could therefore be rather tunable.
evidence: This is an inference from the sensitivity of critical phenomena.

claim: This feature would appear to be favourable for the control of the formation of biomolecular condensates by the protein homeostasis system.
source: This feature would appear to be favourable for the control of the formation of biomolecular condensates by the protein homeostasis system, and also suggest that protein phase separation could be efficiently modulated pharmacologically.
evidence: This is a speculation about biological implications.

claim: Protein phase separation could be efficiently modulated pharmacologically.
source: This feature would appear to be favourable for the control of the formation of biomolecular condensates by the protein homeostasis system, and also suggest that protein phase separation could be efficiently modulated pharmacologically.
evidence: This is a speculation about therapeutic implications.

claim: Human wild-type α-synuclein and A90C cysteine variants were purified from Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3)-gold.
source: Human wild-type α-synuclein and A90C cysteine variants were purified from Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3)-gold (Agilent Technologies) expressing plasmid pT7-7 encoding for α-synuclein as previously described (Dada et al., 2023; Fusco et al., 2014; Hardenberg et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used, supported by citations.
